question.text: A retired investor receives a monthly pension of Rs. 40,000 and wants to set up a SIP in a balanced mutual fund. Which amount would be a reasonable SIP based on general financial planning guidelines?

answer.text: Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 10,000 per month, after accounting for regular expenses and emergency reserve
No amount - retirees should never do SIP

explanation.text: The Logic: A suitable SIP amount for a retiree on a fixed pension must come out of the genuine monthly surplus — what remains after regular living expenses and after setting aside an emergency reserve. On a Rs. 40,000 monthly pension, committing a moderate slice (roughly 12-25%, i.e., around Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 10,000) leaves headroom for routine expenses and unexpected outflows while still building long-term wealth through disciplined investing. The Trap: "Rs. 40,000 (entire pension)" eliminates the budget for daily living expenses and emergencies — it is unsuitable. "Rs. 30,000" leaves only Rs. 10,000 for all monthly expenses, which is unrealistically tight for most retirees. "No amount — retirees should never do SIP" is wrong; SIPs remain appropriate for retirees when sized to true surplus and matched to risk profile. Note: The cited NISM Series V-B workbook pages (19, 20, 21, 207) support recommending schemes appropriate to investor risk profile, expenses and needs, but do not specify a Rs. 5,000-Rs. 10,000 SIP range against a Rs. 40,000 pension. The framing above reflects general financial-planning suitability practice rather than a workbook-stated numeric rule.
